tier_reason: The README Benchmarks table (Linux kernel, 92,916 files) shows ngi vs rg vs grep for 5 patterns: 27/42/71/90/95 ms vs rg 160-174 ms, which is 1.7x-5.9x vs rg and 13x-69x vs grep, plus 13/13 match parity. These are first-party numbers. The repo has no benchmark script (only src/ and tests/), and no CPU, rustc/rg version, run count or cache state is given, so the tier is C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the benchmark; README install instructions use `cargo build --release`; no rustc or ripgrep version stated
corrections.caveats: First-party README benchmark on a named corpus (Linux kernel). The repo has no benchmark harness, and no hardware, rustc/ripgrep version, run count or warm/cold cache state is given. Timings exclude the one-time index build (16 s, 146 MB index for the Linux kernel per README). ngi delegates the regex matching itself to ripgrep; the win comes from trigram pre-filtering of candidate files, and the README says it only helps on selective queries (under 10% of files matching).

notes: The numbers match the README exactly. ngi wraps ripgrep (it pre-filters candidates, then rg does the matching), so it is an indexed front-end, not a faster regex engine. It has 21 stars, an MIT license, and its last commit was 2026-03-24.

tier_reason: The README Benchmark table on git.git shows mean 0.0405 s (trigrep) vs 0.0640 s (ripgrep) vs 0.5990 s (grep), stated as ~1.58x and ~14.79x. The harness scripts/benchmark.sh is public, but no CPU model or rustc version is stated. These are first-party numbers with partial methodology, so the tier is C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Release build: `make benchmark` depends on `make release` (cargo build --workspace --release), and the script runs target/release/trigrep; no rustc version or RUSTFLAGS stated
corrections.caveats: No license: there is no LICENSE file and no license field in either Cargo.toml, so usability is reference. CPU model not stated. The script times each run with `/usr/bin/time -p` (10 ms resolution) over 20 samples. trigrep and ripgrep have the same median (0.0500 s), so the ~1.58x gap exists only in the mean. Index build time is excluded (search-only scope).

notes: The claim matches the README exactly. The win is marginal: the medians are equal, and the timer resolution is close to the measured times. It has 46 stars and its last commit was 2026-04-30.

tier_reason: The README shows Google Benchmark output from benchmarks/to_ascii.cpp: Ada 1504 ns vs ICU (uidna nameToASCII) 1898 ns, with the compiler (LLVM 14) and CPU (Apple M1 Max) stated. The documented build (`cmake -D ADA_IDNA_BENCHMARKS=ON -B build`) defaults to Release with C++20 via cmake/idna-flags.cmake, so the flags are pinned by public build files. This matches the accepted precedent for CMake default-Release builds.

corrections.caveats: Category fit is imperfect: this is IDNA/UTS #46 domain-name processing, not raw UTF-8 validation or transcoding. There is only one README micro-benchmark, over a fixed list of 6 sample domain names (benchmarks/to_ascii.cpp), and the ICU version is not stated. The gain is modest (~1.26x).

notes: The numbers match the README (1.26x derived). The repo ships LICENSE-APACHE and LICENSE-MIT, and the README says it is dual-licensed; GitHub reports only Apache-2.0. It has 69 stars and its last commit was 2026-08-24.

tier_reason: The code (benchmarks/run_utf16_benchmark.py, patches/utf16-simd-milestone.patch, external/baselines/clausecker_lemire/utf16validate_cl.cpp), compiler, flags and CPU (Apple M1) are all public. But the harness does not isolate the baseline. Timing is whole-process via Python subprocess. The simdutf wrapper reads the whole file with std::ifstream into a zero-filled vector before validating, while Parabix streams through ReadSourceKernel. The authors' own docs/benchmark_methodology.md §6 says I/O is not equalized. The numbers come from the authors of the measured kernel and do not cleanly measure simdutf's validator, so the tier is C, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Apple M1, single thread, valid input, whole-process wall clock (median of 7). Raw: Parabix 2900-3760 MiB/s vs simdutf 1824-2532 MiB/s, about 1.18x-2.0x (the page's 'Speedup vs simd_t1' column shows simdutf at 0.50x-0.85x). Overhead-adjusted: Parabix 5075-5205 MiB/s vs simdutf 1883-2600 MiB/s, about 2.0x-2.7x (derived from page data). The student project's README headline is '~2.3-2.5x adjusted' (Apple 2.33x/2.34x, CSIL QEMU x86-64 2.42x/2.52x on the default dataset).
corrections.workload: UTF-16LE validation of 128/256 MiB generated corpora (cjk, default, emoji_heavy, english_ascii_heavy, european_accented, mixed_multilingual, south_asian), valid input, single thread, median of 7 runs after 2 warmups. Timed as whole-process wall clock (includes process startup, file reading and, for Parabix, pipeline load), with an 'adjusted' column that subtracts a fixed per-process overhead measured on a tiny input.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Apple clang 21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101) with Homebrew LLVM 16.0.6 as the Parabix JIT backend. Parabix is built as CMake Release by scripts/setup_parabix.sh. The simdutf v9.0.0 wrapper is built with `c++ -O3 -std=c++17` by scripts/setup_clausecker_lemire.sh. The x86-64 leg used GCC 13.3.0 inside a QEMU guest (simdutf SSE4.2 'westmere' path).
corrections.caveats: The benchmarked UTF-16 validator is not in this repo. It is tools/utf16validate, added by patches/utf16-simd-milestone.patch in the unlicensed, 0-star student repo dakshkashyap/cmpt479-project-group8. That patch is applied to Parabix commit f0369dd from the SFU GitLab (cs-git-research.cs.sfu.ca/cameron/parabix-devel), and that commit is absent from this GitHub mirror (last commit 2021-08-10). I/O is not equalized between the tools (the authors' docs/benchmark_methodology.md §6 says so). The simdutf wrapper reads the whole file into a zero-filled std::vector via ifstream before validating, and runs are timed whole-process. The measured simdutf throughput therefore reflects the wrapper's I/O path more than simdutf's kernel. The headline 2.3-2.5x is overhead-adjusted; the raw gap is 1.18x-2.0x. The x86-64 leg ran in a QEMU guest ('not a physical Ice Lake CPU'). Parabix itself is OSL-3.0 (copyleft; LLVM files under the LLVM Release License). Category: UTF-16, not UTF-8.

notes: The adjusted numbers are on the page, but the comparison pits a streaming Parabix CLI against a simdutf CLI wrapper that reads the whole file first, so it likely measures I/O, not simdutf's validation kernel. The orchestrator may want to drop this record or re-point it at the student repo. The license is not missing: the mirror README declares OSL-3.0 and ships OSL3.0.txt (GitHub reports NOASSERTION).
